$comment: California commercial statutes. These are the provisions that override ordinary contract drafting when a California party or a California consumer is involved — automatic renewal, choice of law for employees, releases, and service provider data terms.

clauses.title: California Automatic Renewal Requirements
clauses.rationale: California's automatic renewal law is prescriptive about presentation, consent, and cancellation. Non-compliant renewals can be treated as unconditional gifts, and the statute carries a private right of action.
clauses.body: Where the renewal in <<xr:msa_renewal>> reaches a California consumer or small business offering, California's [[automatic renewal law]] requires that the renewal terms be presented clearly and conspicuously in visual proximity to the acceptance, that consent be affirmative and separate from acceptance of general terms, that an acknowledgment with the terms and cancellation method be sent after the transaction, that advance notice be given before a renewal following a free or discounted trial, and that cancellation be available by the same medium used to sign up and be no more difficult than signing up. Goods delivered under a non-compliant automatic renewal may be treated as an unconditional gift.
defects: AB 2863 was signed in September 2024 and applies to contracts entered into, amended, or extended on or after 1 July 2025 — more than a year before this check. The clause describes the pre-amendment regime and omits all of it: free-to-pay conversions brought into scope, the new annual reminder notice, the click-to-cancel requirement and its voice equivalent, and the duty to retain consent verification records for three years or one year after termination, whichever is longer.

The clause is not wrong about the old law. It is silent about the current law, which is the more dangerous failure for a compliance clause: it reads as a complete statement of the regime and is a year out of date.
clauses.verificationNote: Checked by web search only against 3 independent sources; no source document was opened. Defect types: omitted-requirement, stale.

clauses.title: California Choice of Law Limits
clauses.rationale: A commercial choice-of-law clause is generally enforceable between businesses, but it does not carry over to individuals working in California — which is where companies with contractor networks get caught.
clauses.body: Between businesses, a governing law clause is generally enforceable, and California expressly permits parties to a contract of at least a quarter million dollars to choose California law regardless of connection. That freedom does not extend to individuals: [[Labor Code §925|labor code 925]] makes a non-California forum or choice of law voidable at the election of any employee — and, in practice, of any misclassified contractor — who primarily works in California. Where individuals perform under this Agreement in California, do not rely on the selected forum to reach them.
defects: "the protection reaches an employee "who primarily works in California"" — the statutory test is an employee who primarily RESIDES AND WORKS in California. Dropping the residence conjunct widens the rule to anyone working here, which is the same defect already confirmed in ea_ca_925 — it has propagated across clauses.

Section 925 does not apply where the employee was in fact individually represented by a lawyer who was involved in negotiating the forum or choice-of-law term. That is the one lawful route to a non-California forum, and the clause omits it entirely — so it tells the reader the door is shut when the statute leaves it open.
clauses.verificationNote: Checked by web search only against 3 independent sources; no source document was opened. Defect types: overstated-scope, omitted-qualifier.

clauses.title: California Anti-Indemnity Limits
clauses.rationale: California voids broad-form indemnity in construction contracts. A clause copied from a general commercial template is unenforceable in this context and can invalidate the additional insured position with it.
clauses.body: California voids any provision in a construction contract purporting to indemnify a party against liability arising from its own sole negligence or willful misconduct, and separately limits a subcontractor's indemnity of a general contractor for the general contractor's active negligence. The indemnity in <<xr:msa_indemnity_mutual>> is limited accordingly. Additional insured endorsements are subject to parallel restrictions, so a broad-form indemnity paired with a broad-form endorsement may fail on both.
defects: Section 2782.05 applies to contracts entered into on or after 1 January 2013. The clause states the limit with no temporal boundary, so it is asserted of contracts it does not reach.

Section 2782.05 also voids the subcontractor’s indemnity to the extent claims arise from work outside the subcontractor’s contractual scope. That is a third protection, independent of active negligence, and the clause omits it — a subcontractor relying on this clause would not know to raise it.
clauses.verificationNote: Checked by web search only against 3 independent sources; no source document was opened. This clause was a control: the defect detectors predicted it clean and it is not. Defect types: omitted-qualifier, omitted-requirement.

clauses.title: Section 1542 Waiver in Settlements
clauses.benchmark: Present in 93% of California settlement and release agreements
clauses.rationale: A general release governed by California law does not reach unknown claims unless Section 1542 is expressly waived, quoting the statute.
clauses.body: Any release given under or in connection with this Agreement shall expressly waive [[Civil Code §1542|section 1542]], quoting it in full, or it will not extend to claims the releasing party did not know or suspect to exist at the time — which is ordinarily the principal reason for taking the release.
defects: "a release must expressly waive §1542, quoting it in full" — The clause states a drafting convention as a rule of law. Section 1542 does not by its terms require a release to quote the statute — that rests on secondary sources here, not on any primary text this repo has opened. What the case law does establish is that what matters is conscious understanding of what is being given up, not any particular form of words.

"otherwise the release will not extend to unknown claims" — The stated consequence is not automatic. Winet enforced an express §1542 waiver against a counsel-advised commercial party; Casey’s protection against inadvertent waiver by mere recital is strongest in personal-injury settings with unrepresented claimants.

The clause gives no signal that the outcome turns on the releasing party’s conscious understanding and on whether they were advised — the facts Winet actually rested on. A clause that says "quote it or unknown claims survive" tells the drafter to get the words right and nothing about the circumstances that decide the case.

Section 1542 was amended effective 1 January 2019. A clause instructing the drafter to quote the section without saying which version invites a stale quotation, which is the failure the instruction exists to prevent.
clauses.verificationNote: Re-checked against the full opinion text of Winet v. Price on CourtListener, which corrected an earlier mischaracterisation of the holding taken from law-firm summaries. CourtListener is a republisher, not the court, so this remains below the two-primary standard.

clauses.title: Proposition 65 Warnings
clauses.rationale: Enforced largely through private actions with fee recovery, which makes it a volume business for plaintiffs' counsel. Allocating responsibility up the supply chain is the practical defense.
clauses.body: Goods sold into California may require a Proposition 65 warning where they expose a person to a listed chemical. Allocate responsibility for determining whether a warning is required, for the warning's content and placement including on the product page, and for indemnity if a claim follows. Enforcement is primarily by private plaintiffs who recover attorney's fees, and a warning that is present but non-conforming is treated as no warning at all.
defects: "a warning that is present but non-conforming is treated as no warning at all" — the safe-harbor regulations define warnings deemed clear and reasonable; a non-conforming warning loses the safe harbor rather than being void as such

Proposition 65 does not apply to a business employing fewer than 10 employees. For a product built for small companies this is the single most consequential qualifier in the statute, and the clause states the duty with no threshold at all — so the reader most likely to be exempt is told they are covered.

The exemption does not travel upstream: a manufacturer or distributor selling through an exempt small vendor still owes the consumer a warning. A clause that allocates responsibility between the parties without this cannot allocate it correctly.

The safe-harbor warning content and methods were amended effective 30 August 2018. The clause tells the reader to allocate responsibility for "the warning’s content and placement" without pointing at the regulations that define what content is safe.
clauses.verificationNote: Checked by web search only against 3 independent sources; no source document was opened. This clause was a control: the defect detectors predicted it clean and it is not. Defect types: omitted-qualifier, omitted-requirement.

clauses.title: CCPA Service Provider Terms
clauses.rationale: Service provider status is not a label — it depends on specific contract terms being present. Without them the transfer is a sale, which triggers opt-out rights the business almost certainly has not built.
clauses.body: To qualify as a service provider rather than a recipient of a sale of personal information, this Addendum must state the specific business purposes for processing, prohibit selling or sharing the personal information, prohibit retaining, using, or disclosing it outside the direct business relationship or for any purpose other than the specified services, prohibit combining it with information from other sources except as permitted, require notice if the service provider can no longer meet its obligations, and grant the business the right to take reasonable steps to stop and remediate unauthorized use. The roles stated in <<xr:dpa_roles>> depend on these terms being present.

clauses.title: Sensitive Personal Information
clauses.rationale: California created a distinct category with its own right to limit use, and it captures data most businesses do not think of as sensitive — precise geolocation and contents of messages among them.
clauses.body: Sensitive personal information under California law includes government identifiers, financial account credentials, precise geolocation, racial or ethnic origin, religious beliefs, union membership, the contents of mail and messages, genetic and biometric data, and health, sex life, or sexual orientation data. Consumers may direct that its use be limited to what is necessary to provide the service. Identify in the processing description at <<xr:dpa_scope>> whether any sensitive category is in scope, and implement the limitation right where it is.

clauses.title: Deletion Down the Chain
clauses.rationale: The deletion obligation flows to every subprocessor, and a business cannot satisfy a consumer request it has no mechanism to push downstream.
clauses.body: On a consumer deletion request, the {{selfLabel}} shall delete the personal information and direct each subprocessor engaged under <<xr:dpa_subprocessors>> to do the same, unless a statutory exception applies. Maintain a record of the request, the action taken, and any exception relied on. Deletion obligations reach backups on the ordinary cycle as provided in <<xr:dpa_deletion>>.

clauses.title: California Prevailing Wage
clauses.rationale: Public works reaches further than most contractors expect, including privately built projects that receive public subsidy, and the penalties are per worker per day.
clauses.body: If any part of this work is a public work under California law — including private projects paid for in whole or part with public funds — prevailing wage rates apply, contractors and subcontractors must be registered with the Department of Industrial Relations, certified payroll records must be submitted electronically, and apprenticeship requirements attach. Confirm public works status before pricing. Penalties are assessed per worker per day of violation, and the awarding body may withhold payment until cured.

clauses.title: Worker Classification Flow-Down
clauses.benchmark: Present in 31% of California services agreements; more common where the provider uses a contractor bench
clauses.rationale: A customer can inherit joint employer exposure for a provider's misclassified workforce, and the indemnity is the only practical protection.
clauses.body: The {{selfLabel}} represents that individuals performing the Services are properly classified under California law, including the [[ABC test|abc test]] where it applies, that all wages, overtime, meal and rest premiums, and business expense reimbursements have been paid, and that required workers' compensation coverage is in place. The {{selfLabel}} shall indemnify the {{counterLabel}} against claims arising from misclassification of its personnel, and this indemnity sits within the carve-outs at <<xr:msa_liability_carveouts>>.
